title: In 2006, A Florida Man Sifting Mud Out Of Fossil Clams Found 83 Tiny Glass Beads Inside. They Had Been Blasted Out By A Meteorite Impact - Futura-Sciences
excerpt: He was looking for microscopic shells in a Sarasota County quarry. What he found sat in a drawer for years before anyone understood where it came from.
content:
He was looking for microscopic shells in a Sarasota County quarry. What he found sat in a drawer for years before anyone understood where it came from.

In the summer of 2006, Mike Meyer was doing the kind of work that never makes the news. An undergraduate at the University of South Florida, he had joined a fieldwork project in a quarry in Sarasota County, on Florida’s Gulf Coast, led by Roger Portell of the Florida Museum of Natural History. The students were collecting fossil clams, and Meyer’s job was to sieve the sediment packed inside them.

He was hunting for foraminifera, tiny single-celled organisms whose microscopic shells are common in old marine sediments. Instead, among the grains, he kept spotting something else: minuscule glassy spheres, smaller than grains of salt. “They really stood out,” he later recalled.

Meyer ended up collecting 83 of them. Most were sealed inside the shells of southern quahogs, a species of clam, and they turned up at four different depths in the quarry. For years, nobody knew exactly what they were.

The answer finally came in a study published in 2019 in the journal Meteoritics and Planetary Science. Meyer, by then an assistant professor at Harrisburg University in Pennsylvania, had analyzed the beads with Portell and Peter Harries of North Carolina State University. Their conclusion: the spheres were microtektites, droplets of rock melted by a meteorite impact, flung into the atmosphere and cooled into glass before raining back down.

“It did blow my mind,” Meyer said.

An impact nobody has found

According to the researchers, they are the first microtektites ever documented in Florida, and possibly the first ever recovered from inside fossil shells. Portell estimates they are “somewhere around 2 to 3 million years old.”

The beads also contain unusually high levels of sodium, which suggests the impact happened relatively close by, perhaps on the Florida Platform itself or near a large source of salt or seawater. The crater, if it exists, has never been found.

The clams, it turns out, made perfect time capsules. After the impact, the glass beads settled on the seafloor, were swept inside the empty shells along with the sediment, and stayed sealed there for millions of years. “It’s a nice way of preserving specimens,” Portell said.

The quarry where it all happened no longer exists in its original form: it is now part of a housing development. “Such is the nature of Florida,” Meyer said.

Space rocks have a habit of hiding in plain sight. A man in Michigan once used a meteorite as a doorstop for 30 years without knowing it.
